Welcome to MLPToolbox’s Documentation!

MLPToolbox is designed to train Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) using reverse-mode Algorithmic Differentiation (AD) and features an advanced Gradient Annealing algorithm to mitigate gradient pathologies.

Understanding Gradient Annealing & Lambda

In standard PINNs, the total loss is a composite of data-fit terms (\(L_i\), e.g., boundary conditions, reference data) and physics residual terms (\(L_r\), e.g., Navier-Stokes equations):

\[L(\theta) = L_r(\theta) + \sum_{i=1}^{M} \lambda_i L_i(\theta)\]

The Problem: Gradient Pathologies

As discussed in Wang et al. (2020), the back-propagated gradients of the PDE residual (\(\nabla_\theta L_r\)) are often orders of magnitude larger than the data gradients (\(\nabla_\theta L_i\)). This causes the optimizer to focus solely on minimizing the physics residual while ignoring the boundary/initial conditions, leading to erroneous predictions.

The Solution: Adaptive Lambda (\(\lambda_i\))

MLPToolbox implements Paper Algorithm 1 to dynamically update \(\lambda_i\) during training. Instead of manually tuning \(\lambda_i\), the trainer tracks gradient statistics:

  1. Instantaneous Lambda (\(\hat{\lambda}_i\)): Computed as the ratio between the maximum absolute gradient of the physics residual and the mean absolute gradient of the data term:

    \[\hat{\lambda}_i = \frac{\max_\theta |\nabla_\theta L_r|}{\overline{|\nabla_\theta L_i|}}\]

  2. Exponential Moving Average (EMA): To prevent oscillations, the actual weight is smoothed using an EMA coefficient (\(\alpha\)):

    \[\lambda_i \leftarrow (1 - \alpha)\lambda_i + \alpha \hat{\lambda}_i\]

How it affects the loss: By scaling \(L_i\) by \(\lambda_i\), the effective learning rate of the data-fit terms is scaled up, forcing the network to respect boundary conditions and reference data even when the physics residuals are extremely stiff.

Core API Components

MLPToolbox is modular. A typical workflow involves constructing a Network, defining Losses, configuring an Optimizer and Annealer, and passing them to the Trainer.

The Optimizer: CAdam

A standard Adam optimizer implementation.

CAdam(
    mlpdouble learning_rate = 1e-3,
    mlpdouble beta1 = 0.9,
    mlpdouble beta2 = 0.999,
    mlpdouble epsilon = 1e-8
)

The Annealer: CGradientAnnealer

The annealer automatically balances the loss terms. It is configured using the AnnealerConfig struct.

AnnealerConfig Parameters:

  • alpha: Default 0.9. Controls the EMA smoothing. A higher value makes \(\lambda\) react faster to gradient changes, while a lower value smooths it out. 0.9 is recommended by the paper.

  • lambda_init: Default 1.0. The initial \(\lambda\) for all data terms.

  • lambda_max: Default 1e4. Crucial parameter. If your non-dimensionalization introduces large scaling coefficients, the physics gradients will be massive, driving \(\hat{\lambda}_i\) to infinity. The hard clamp prevents gradient explosion.

  • lambda_min: Default 1e-4. Prevents a data term from being completely ignored.

  • n_data_terms: Automatically calculated by the CMLPTrainer during Build() as n_reference_losses + n_boundary_losses.

The Trainer: CMLPTrainer

The trainer orchestrates the AD tape, mini-batching, MPI synchronization, and the fast/slow path gradient evaluations.

TrainerConfig Parameters:

  • batch_size: The number of reference data points processed per gradient step.

  • physics_batch_size: The number of collocation points processed per step. Performance Note: Computing Hessians (2nd derivatives) for momentum equations is memory and CPU intensive. Keep this between 32 and 128.

  • use_annealer: Set to true to enable the gradient pathology mitigation.

  • annealer_update_freq: Performance Note. Computing \(\hat{\lambda}_i\) requires \(N+1\) reverse sweeps of the AD tape. Setting this to 10 means the expensive “Slow Path” only runs every 10 steps. On the other 9 steps, the trainer uses a “Fast Path” (1 sweep) with the cached \(\lambda\) values.

  • max_grad_norm: If > 0.0, applies global gradient clipping to prevent NaNs.

Example: 2D Lid-Driven Cavity

The following C++ snippet demonstrates how to configure the MLPToolbox API to solve the steady-state incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a 2D lid-driven cavity.

#include "CNeuralNetwork.hpp"
#include "CAdam.hpp"
#include "CGradientAnnealer.hpp"
#include "CMLPTrainer.hpp"
#include "CPhysicsLoss.hpp"
#include "CMeanSquaredErrorLoss.hpp"

using namespace MLPToolbox;

void train_cavity() {
    // 1. Network Definition
    std::vector<std::size_t> architecture = {2, 32, 32, 32, 3};
    CNeuralNetwork net(architecture);
    net.SetActivationFunction(net.GetnLayers() - 1, "linear");
    net.SetInputName(0, "x"); net.SetInputName(1, "y");
    net.SetOutputName(0, "u"); net.SetOutputName(1, "v"); net.SetOutputName(2, "p");

    // 2. Optimizer & Annealer Configuration
    CAdam optimizer(1e-3, 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8);
    AnnealerConfig anneal_cfg;
    anneal_cfg.alpha = 0.9;
    anneal_cfg.lambda_max = 1e4;

    // 3. Trainer Configuration
    TrainerConfig trainer_cfg;
    trainer_cfg.max_epochs         = 500;
    trainer_cfg.batch_size         = 128;
    trainer_cfg.physics_batch_size = 32;  // Keep small for Hessian memory
    trainer_cfg.use_annealer       = true;
    trainer_cfg.annealer_update_freq = 10; // Run slow path every 10 steps
    trainer_cfg.shuffle_per_epoch  = true;

    CMLPTrainer trainer(net, std::move(optimizer), anneal_cfg, trainer_cfg);

    // 4. Set Training Data (L_i)
    std::vector<std::vector<mlpdouble>> X_train, Y_train;
    // LoadSU2CSV_NonDim(...); populates X_train, Y_train
    trainer.SetTrainingData(X_train, Y_train);
    trainer.AddReferenceLoss(std::make_shared<CMeanSquaredErrorLoss>());

    // 5. Generate Collocation Sets
    std::vector<std::vector<mlpdouble>> interior_pts, top_bc_pts, wall_bc_pts;
    // Populate points here...
    trainer.SetCollocationPoints("interior", interior_pts);
    trainer.SetCollocationPoints("top_bc", top_bc_pts);
    trainer.SetCollocationPoints("wall_bc", wall_bc_pts);

    // 6. Define Physics Equations (L_r)
    CPhysicsEquation eq_cont;
    eq_cont.name = "continuity";
    eq_cont.input_names = {"x", "y"};
    eq_cont.output_names = {"u", "v"};
    eq_cont.requires_jacobian = true;
    eq_cont.residual = [](const PhysicsState& s, const PhysicsData&) -> mlpdouble {
        return s.Jac(0, 0) + s.Jac(1, 1); // du/dx + dv/dy
    };

    auto loss_cont = std::make_shared<CPhysicsLoss>(
        "loss_continuity", net.GetInputVars(), net.GetOutputVars(),
        std::vector<std::string>{}, std::vector<CPhysicsEquation>{eq_cont}
    );
    trainer.AddPhysicsLoss(loss_cont, "interior");

    // 7. Define Boundary Conditions as Physics Losses (L_i)
    CPhysicsEquation eq_top_u;
    eq_top_u.name = "bc_top_u";
    eq_top_u.input_names = {"x", "y"};
    eq_top_u.output_names = {"u"};
    eq_top_u.residual = [](const PhysicsState& s, const PhysicsData&) -> mlpdouble {
        return s.Out(0) - 1.0; // u = 1 on top wall
    };
    auto loss_top_u = std::make_shared<CPhysicsLoss>(
        "loss_top_u", net.GetInputVars(), net.GetOutputVars(),
        std::vector<std::string>{}, std::vector<CPhysicsEquation>{eq_top_u}
    );
    trainer.AddBoundaryLoss(loss_top_u, "top_bc");

    // 8. Initialize MPI and Build
    trainer.EnableMPI();
    trainer.Build();

    // 9. Train
    for (std::size_t epoch = 0; epoch < trainer_cfg.max_epochs; ++epoch) {
        trainer.TrainEpoch();

        // Logging custom history...
        double avg_data_loss = trainer.GetEpochAverageLossRef();
        double avg_phys_loss = trainer.GetEpochAverageLossPhys(0);
        double avg_bc_loss   = trainer.GetEpochAverageLossBC(0);
        double avg_lambda    = trainer.GetEpochAverageLambda(0);
        double avg_total     = trainer.GetEpochAverageLossTotal();
    }
}
